'''baline''' (ba-lēn′), ''n.'' [F., packing-cloth; cf. ''balin'', winnowing-cloth.] A coarse kind of canvas used for packing.

'''balinger†''' (bal′in-jėr), ''n.'' [< ME. ''balinger'', ''balenger'', etc., < OF. ''balengier'', ''ballenjer'', ''baleinier'', orig. a whale-ship (= Pg. ''baleeiro'', a whaler, a whale-ship, = It. ''baleniera'', a pinnace), < ''baleine'', a whale: see ''baleen''.] A small sea-going war-vessel in use in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, and supposed to have been a kind of sloop without forecastle.
{{smaller block|In February, 1417, the king possessed six great ships, eight barges, and ten ''balingers''.
{{right|''Stubbs'', Const. Hist., § 650.}}}}

'''baling-press''' (bā′ling-pres), ''n.'' A power-press employed for compressing soft or fibrous materials, as raw cotton, hay, and cotton and woolen goods, into bales for transportation.

'''balisaur''' (bal′i-sâr), ''n.'' [< Hind. ''bālusūr'', sand-hog, < ''bālu'' (Beng. ''bāli''), sand, + ''sūr'', a hog (cf. Skt. ''sūkara'', a hog).] The common Indian badger, ''Arctonyx collaris'', of the family ''Mustelidæ'' and subfamily ''Melinæ''. {{smaller|It resembles the common European badger of the genus ''Meles'', but is larger, and is, from its technical characteristics, placed in a different genus. It is a true badger, one of several members of the ''Melinæ''. See ''badger''<sup>2</sup>. Also spelled ''balysaur''.}}

'''balise''', ''n.'' See ''balize''.

'''balista''', ''n.'' See ''ballista''.

'''balister<sup>1</sup>†''' (bal′is-tėr), ''n.'' [< ME. ''balester'', < OF. ''balestier'', < LL. ''ballistarius'', one who makes crossbows, a crossbowman, < L. ''ballista'', a crossbow. Cf. ''arcubalister''.] A crossbowman.

'''balk-line''' (bâk′līn), ''n.'' In ''billiards'', a diagonal line cutting off a corner, or a straight line cutting off a uniform space on each side (generally 14 inches), from the main field of the table.

'''balk-staff''' (bâk′stȧf), ''n.'' A quarter-staff.

'''balinger†''' (bal′in-jėr), ''n.''   [< ME. ''balinger'', ''balenger'', etc., < OF. ''balengier'', ''ballenjer'', ''baleinier'', orig. a whale-ship (= Pg. ''baleeiro'', a whaler, a whale-ship, = It. ''baleniera'', a pinnace), < ''baleine'', a whale: see ''baleen''.]   A small sea-going war-vessel in use in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, and supposed to have been a kind of sloop without forecastle. {{smaller block|In February, 1417, the king possessed six great ships, eight barges, and ten ''balingers''. {{right|''Stubbs'', Const. Hist., § 650.}}}} '''baling-press''' (bā′ling-pres), ''n.'' A power-press employed for compressing soft or fibrous materials, as raw cotton, hay, and cotton and woolen goods, into bales for transportation. '''balisaur''' (bal′i-sâr), ''n.''   [< Hind. ''bālusūr'', sand-hog, < ''bālu'' (Beng. ''bāli''), sand, + ''sūr'', a hog (cf. Skt. ''sūkara'', a hog).]   The common Indian badger, ''Arctonyx collaris'', of the family ''Mustelidæ'' and subfamily ''Melinæ''. {{smaller|It resembles the common European badger of the genus ''Meles'', but is larger, and is, from its technical characteristics, placed in a different genus. It is a true badger, one of several members of the ''Melinæ''. See ''badger''2. Also spelled ''balysaur''.}} '''balise''', ''n.'' See ''balize''. '''balista''', ''n.'' See ''ballista''. '''balister1†''' (bal′is-tėr), ''n.''   [< ME. ''balester'', < OF. ''balestier'', < LL. ''ballistarius'', one who makes crossbows, a crossbowman, < L. ''ballista'', a crossbow. Cf. ''arcubalister''.]   A crossbowman. '''balister2†''' (bal′is-tėr), ''n.''   [< OF. ''balestre'', < ML. ''balistra'', a var. of L. ''ballista'', a crossbow (cf. ML. ''balistarius arcus'', a crossbow): see ''ballista''.]   An arbalist or crossbow. Also spelled ''ballister''. '''Balistes''' (ba-lis′tēz), ''n.''   [NL., < L. ''balista'', better ''ballista'', the military engine; so called for the same reason as they are called trigger-fish: [[File:century v01 p0455 c1f1.png|center|310px]] {{c|{{smaller|Trigger-fish (''Balistes capriscus'').}}}} see def.]   A genus of plectognath fishes, typical of the family ''Balistidæ'', containing such species as ''B. capriscus''. {{smaller|They are known as ''trigger-fish'', because one large and sharp first ray of the dorsal fin cannot be pressed down until the second ray is depressed, when the first shuts down as does the hammer of a gun when the trigger is pulled.}} '''balistid''' (ba-lis′tid), ''n.'' A fish of the family ''Balistidæ''. '''Balistidæ''' (ba-lis′ti-dē), ''n. pl.''   [NL., < ''Balistes'' + ''-idæ''.]   A family of fishes, typified by the genus ''Balistes'', adopted by different authors with various limits. {{smaller|(''a'') In Bonaparte’s early system, 1832, a family embracing the ''Balistidæ'', ''Triacanthidæ'', and ''Ostraciontidæ'', and thus equivalent to the ''Sclerodermes'' of Cuvier. (''b'') In Bonaparte’s later systems (1840, etc.), a family embracing the ''Balistidæ'' and ''Triacanthidæ'', thus equivalent to the suborder ''Sclerodermi'' of Gill. (''c'') In Swainson’s system, a family including all the plectognath fishes. (''d'') In Gill’s system, a family of scleroderm plectognaths with reduced rhombiform or more or less spiniform dermal appendages; a compressed body; teeth few in number and more or less compressed; a long pelvis, compressed and arcuate, with the tip sometimes prominent and sometimes concealed; and no paired ventral fins or spines. The species are numerous in tropical and subtropical seas, and are divided into three subfamilies, the ''Balistinæ'', ''Monacanthinæ'', and ''Psilocephalinæ''. See these words. Species are known as ''trigger-fish'', ''file-fish'', etc.}} '''Balistina''' (bal-is-tī′nä̤), ''n. pl.''   [NL., < ''Balistes'' + ''-ina''.]   In Günther’s classification of fishes, the second group of his family ''Sclerodermi'', identical with the family ''Balistidæ'' of recent authors. '''Balistinæ''' (bal-is-tī′nē), ''n. pl.''   [NL., < ''Balistes'' + ''-inæ''.]   '''1.''' A subfamily of balistoid fishes having few vertebræ (17), an anterior dorsal fin consisting of 3 (rarely 2) spines, of which the first is enlarged and the second locks it in erection, branchial apertures behind the eyes, a compressed ovate form, and rhombiform scales. {{smaller|The most common English names of the species are ''file-fish'' and ''trigger-fish''. The flesh is generally but little esteemed, and may even be poisonous; but in some places, as in Bermuda, one of the species of the genus ''Balistes'' is highly esteemed and locally called ''turbot''. The skin is used for filing and as a substitute for sandpaper. See cut under ''Balistes''.}} '''2.''' In early systems of classification, a subfamily embracing the ''Balistidæ'' and ''Triacanthidæ'', and equivalent to the suborder ''Sclerodermi'' of Gill.—'''3.''' In some systems, a subfamily equivalent to the family ''Balistidæ'' of Gill. '''balistine''' (ba-lis′tin), ''n.'' A fish of the subfamily ''Balistinæ''. '''balistoid''' (ba-lis′toid), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [< ''Balistes'' + ''-oid''.]   '''I.''' ''a.'' Pertaining to or having the characters of the ''Balistidæ''. '''II.''' ''n.'' A balistid. '''balistraria''' (bal-is-trā′ri-ä̤), ''n.''   [ML., < ''balistra'', a form of ''ballista'', a crossbow: see ''balister''2.]   In ''old fort.'': (''a'') A loophole or aperture in the wall of a fortification, or in a wooden hoarding temporarily put up for defense, through which crossbowmen might discharge their bolts. See ''loophole'', and compare ''archeria''. (''b'') A room in which balisters or crossbows were kept. '''balize, balise''' (ba-lēz′), ''n.''   [< F. ''balise'' = Sp. Pg. ''baliza'', Sp. also ''balisa'', ''valiza'', a beacon, buoy, sea-mark; origin unknown.]   A sea-mark or beacon at the mouth of a river or the entrance to a harbor; a barrel-buoy, a pole surmounted by a peculiar flag or other object, etc. '''balk1, baulk''' (bâk), ''n.''   [< ME. ''balk'', ''balke'', < AS. ''balca'', a ridge, = OS. ''balco'' = OFries. ''balka'' = OD. ''balke'', D. ''balk'' = MLG. ''balke'', a beam, balance, corn-loft, LG. ''balke'', corn-loft, = OHG. ''balcho'', ''balko'' (> It. ''balco'', a beam, > ''balcone'', > E. ''balcony'', q. v.), MHG. ''balke'', G. ''balke'', ''balken'', a beam, bar; also, with diff. formative, AS. ''balc'' (once), a ridge, = Icel. ''bālkr'', ''bōlkr'' = Sw. ''balk'' = Norw. ''balk'', ''bolk'', beam, bar, partition, division, = Dan. ''balk'', ridge, partition; AS. ''bolca'', gangway, = Icel. ''bjálki'' = Sw. ''bjälke'', ''bjelke'' = Dan. ''bjælke'', a beam; cf. AS. ''bælc'', covering; perhaps akin to Gr. φάλαγξ, a beam, pole, log, trunk, block: see ''phalanx''.]   '''1.''' A ridge; especially, a ridge left unplowed in the body of a field, or between fields; an uncultivated strip of land serving as a boundary, often between pieces of ground held by different tenants. {{smaller|The latter use originated in the open-field system (which see, under ''field''). [Common in provincial English and Scotch.]}} {{smaller block|Dikeres and deluers digged vp the ''balkes''. {{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), vi. 109.}}}} {{smaller block|Green ''balks'' and furrow’d lands. {{right|''Cowper'', Retirement.}}}} {{smaller block|The property consisted of 2,752 acres, which were divided into 3,509 strips of land set at every possible angle, from nine to thirty feet wide and about nine or ten chains long, with a grass path called a ''balk'' between each. {{right|''Nineteenth Century'', XIX. 902.}}}} '''2.''' A piece missed in plowing. Hence—'''3†.''' An omission; an exception. {{smaller block|The mad steele about doth fiercely fly, Not sparing wight, ne leaving any ''balke''. {{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., VI. xi. 16.}}}} '''4.''' A blunder; a failure or miscarriage: as, to make a ''balk''; you have made a bad ''balk'' of it. [Now chiefly colloq.] Hence—'''5.''' In ''base-ball'', a motion made by the pitcher as if to pitch the ball, but without actually doing so.—'''6†.''' A barrier in one’s way; an obstacle or stumbling-block.—'''7.''' A check or defeat; a disappointment. {{smaller block|A ''balk'' to the confidence of the bold undertaker. {{right|''South.''}}}} 8. In ''coal-mining'', a more or less sudden thinning out, for a certain distance, of a bed of coal; a nip or want.—'''9.''' A beam or piece of timber of considerable length and thickness. {{smaller|Specifically—(''a'') A cross-beam in the roof of a house which unites and supports the rafters; a tie-beam. In old-fashioned one-story houses of Scotland, Ireland, and the North of England these tie-beams were often exposed, and boards or peeled saplings called ''cabers'' were laid across them, forming a kind of loft often called the ''balks''. From these exposed tie-beams or from the cabers articles were often suspended. [Prov. Eng. and Scotch.]}} {{smaller block|Tubbes hanging in the ''balkes''. {{right|''Chaucer'', Miller’s Tale, l. 440.}}}} {{smaller block|The stiffest ''balk'' bends more or less; all joists creak. {{right|''Carlyle'', French Rev., II. i. 12.}}}} {{smaller block|(''b'') ''Milit.'', one of the beams connecting the successive supports of a trestle-bridge or bateau-bridge. (''c'') In ''carp.'', a squared timber, long or short; a large timber in a frame, floor, etc.; a square log.}} '''10.''' The beam of a balance. [Obsolete, except in dialectal usage.]—'''11.''' In ''billiards'', the space between the cushion of the table and the balk-line. A ball inside this space is said to be ''in balk''.—'''12.''' A long wooden or iron table on which paper is laid in the press-room of a printing-office.—'''13.''' A set of stout stakes surrounded by netting or wickerwork for catching fish.   ''N. E. D.'' [Prov. Eng.]—'''14.''' The stout rope at the top of fishing-nets by which they are fastened one to another in a fleet. [In Cornwall, ''balch''.] ''N. E. D.'' '''balk1, baulk''' (bâk), ''v.''   [< ME. ''balken'', make a balk in land, that is, leave a strip or ridge of land unplowed, < ''balk'', a ridge: see ''balk''1, ''n.'' Cf. Norw. ''balka'', do clumsy work.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1†.''' To make a balk or ridge in plowing; make a ridge in by leaving a strip unplowed. {{smaller block|To tille a felde man must have diligence, And ''balk'' it not. {{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 8.}}}} Hence —'''2†.''' To leave untouched generally; omit; pass over; neglect; shun. {{smaller block|''Balk'' logic with acquaintance that you have. {{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., i. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|By reason of ye contagion then in London, we ''baulked'' the inns. {{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, Oct. 10, 1641.}}}} '''3.''' To place a balk in the way of; hence, to hinder; thwart; frustrate; disappoint. {{smaller block|My Sport is always ''balkt'', or cut short — I stumble over the game I would pursue. {{right|''Congreve'', Old Batchelor, iv. 5.}}}} {{smaller block|Alike to the citizen and to the legislator, home experiences daily supply proofs that the conduct of human beings ''balks'' calculation. {{right|''H. Spencer'', Sins of Legislators, ii.}}}} '''4†.''' To miss by error or inadvertence. {{smaller block|You cannot ''baulk'' your Road without the hazard of drowning. {{right|''Feltham'', Low Countries (1677), p. 46. (''N. E. D.'')}}}} '''5†.''' To heap up so as to form a balk or ridge. [Rare.] {{smaller block|Ten thousand bold Scots, two-and-twenty knights, ''Balk’d'' in their own blood, did Sir Walter see On Holmedon’s plains. {{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., i. 1.}}}} [Some editors read ''bak’d'' in this passage.] ='''Syn. 3.''' {{smaller|''Foil'', ''Thwart'', etc. See ''frustrate''.}} '''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.'''
